items.title: The Quiet Growth of Heat Pumps

paras.label: A
paras.text: Heat pumps move heat rather than create it. In winter, a heat pump draws warmth from the outside air and releases it indoors. Because the device moves energy instead of burning fuel, it can deliver three or four units of heat for each unit of electricity it uses.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Sales have risen sharply in northern Europe since 2015. Norway now has more heat pumps per household than any other country. Engineers once believed the technology failed in very cold weather, but modern designs work well at minus twenty degrees.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The main obstacle is the upfront price. Installing a system can cost twice as much as a new gas boiler, although running costs are usually lower. Some governments offer grants to cover part of the installation cost.

items.title: Why Cities Are Rethinking the Bus

paras.label: A
paras.text: For decades, city planners treated the bus as a last resort for people without cars. Routes were long and slow, and timetables were difficult to read. As a result, many riders switched to private vehicles whenever they could afford one.

paras.label: B
paras.text: In the 2010s several cities redesigned their networks from scratch. Instead of many winding routes, they created fewer, straighter lines with buses every ten minutes. Houston, for example, increased weekend ridership after its redesign without adding any new buses.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Technology has also changed the experience. Real-time arrival screens reduce the stress of waiting, and contactless payment speeds up boarding. However, researchers note that frequency matters far more to passengers than any app.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Critics argue that bus lanes take space away from drivers and hurt local shops. Studies from several European cities suggest the opposite: shoppers who arrive by bus or on foot visit more often and spend more over a month.
